Here is how the two raises compare across the dimensions that matter most for your Series A goal.

£750k gives you more runway to reach £50k MRR
You are currently at £18k MRR growing 10% month-on-month. At that rate you hit £50k in roughly 10 months. Eight months of runway means you are cutting it very close without more capital. £750k buys you the buffer to absorb a growth slowdown, hire ahead of the curve, or survive a bad month. £250k extends runway but leaves little margin for error.

£250k means less dilution now, which protects your Series A valuation
Seed dilution directly affects how attractive your cap table looks to Series A investors. A smaller raise at this stage preserves more equity for the next round, which can improve terms. The trade-off is that you are betting your growth rate holds.

The mechanism that matters most is growth rate consistency
Both options work through the same path: capital raised drives runway, runway enables MRR growth, MRR growth determines Series A readiness. The question is not really £250k versus £750k in isolation. It is how confident you are that 10% month-on-month growth continues without additional resource. If growth is fragile, the extra capital in £750k is insurance. If growth is robust, £250k may be sufficient and cheaper in equity terms.

The model has no cost or budget factor yet
Your burn rate determines how far each raise actually stretches. £750k at £30k/month burn is 25 months. At £60k/month it is 12. Without knowing your current burn, the runway estimates in the model are rough. That is the single most useful number you could add right now.

raw_response.assistant_text:
The core trade-off is leadership depth versus delivery throughput. One tech lead gives you better architectural decisions and reduces the risk of your senior developer becoming a bottleneck, but adds less raw coding capacity. Two juniors add hands but increase coordination overhead and lean harder on your senior developer to guide them.

Three things are worth thinking through before running the numbers:

Your senior developer's current load is the pivot point. If they are already stretched, two juniors could slow the team down rather than speed it up. The model currently estimates their overload risk at 0.5, which is neutral. How close to capacity are they actually running?

Architectural decision quality matters more for a rewrite than for feature work. A rewrite involves structural choices that are hard to reverse. If your team lacks someone who can own those decisions confidently, the cost of getting them wrong compounds over 18 months. The model treats this as an observable factor but has no baseline from your brief.

All three options currently act through the same mechanisms. That means the model cannot yet distinguish between them sharply. The single most useful calibration is how strongly hiring a tech lead actually improves architectural quality in your context. Is your senior developer capable of covering that role, or is there a genuine gap?

That last question would most change the recommendation. How would you rate your senior developer's ability to lead the architectural decisions on this rewrite?
